summary:
No Sivas-specific statute, enforcement programme, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources assembled for this edition. The province of Sivas stands under the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in Sivas is recorded adding prohibitions of its own.

That national framework, as set out in the sources, is as follows. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is, however, no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the Turkish military: a health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and the resulting 'unfit report' can leak and fuel later discrimination in public life. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised; when the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 the anti-LGBTQ provisions were removed from the bill, leaving only symbolic same-sex weddings possible.

Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. Early-2026 press reports recorded that the government considered legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'. Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches in Istanbul, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Blanket bans combined with case-by-case prosecutions under Law No. 2911 form the enforcement climate that provincial authorities in Sivas operate under, as across Turkey.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement climate documented in Istanbul and İzmir is national in scope: blanket bans on Pride marches, mass detentions and prosecutions under Law No. 2911 apply to provincial authorities throughout Turkey, including Sivas, even though no Sivas-specific application of these powers is recorded in the sources.

Turkey's standing in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking, 47th of 49 countries, provides comparative context for the legal position a trans visitor in Sivas would encounter, as does the absence of any comprehensive discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

Trans residents of Sivas can change their legal gender under the national framework, a right available since 1988, but the process requires sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission.

Residents face no statutory protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised.

Openly LGBTQ residents are barred from military service under a health regulation treating homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', with an 'unfit report' that can leak and affect later public-life opportunities.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the draft legislative package reported by Human Rights Watch in October 2025, which would effectively criminalise LGBT people under provisions protecting 'the family' and 'public morals', has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Whether the early-2026 press reports of considered legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' resulted in enacted law is unresolved in the sources.

No source in this inventory documents how Law No. 2911 bans or prosecutions have been applied within Sivas province specifically; the enforcement record cited is from Istanbul and İzmir.
